title: How I would fix all of America’s major problems
gist: Yglesias lays out his idealized policy agenda: a universal age-tapered child cash benefit (baby bonus, paid leave, child care allowance) and a VAT-financed free tier of health care, while arguing US long-term budget problems are now near-term and US violence levels hurt the poor. The preview is cut off by a paywall.

insights.claim: Yglesias argues the US is a rich country with relatively poor public-health outcomes given its prosperity.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Public health underperformance is a policy target with health-sector implications.
insights.locator: Still, I think we can say

insights.claim: Americans in the top half of the income distribution are much richer than Germans, but in the bottom third not so much.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: US inequality means consumption strength is concentrated at the top.
insights.quote: Americans in the top half of the income distribution are much richer than Germans. In the bottom third, not so much.

insights.claim: US long-term budget problems are no longer really long-term and need to be dealt with, Yglesias argues.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Fiscal consolidation (tax increases/spending restraint) is moving onto the near-term agenda; relevant to Treasury supply and rates.

insights.claim: Yglesias says housing problems are relatively straightforward and simple to fix, in contrast to health care, which requires attention to fussy technical details.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Housing supply reform seen as the more tractable policy lever.

insights.claim: US national interest is best advanced through openness to the world and collaboration with other open societies, per Yglesias.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Favors trade and alliance openness over protectionism.

insights.claim: Yglesias proposes unconditional cash benefits for children framed as a universal transfer from non-parents to parents, like public schools, rather than an income-phased anti-poverty program.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Large universal family transfer would be a major fiscal outlay and consumer-demand boost for families.

insights.claim: The proposed benefit would start with a big one-off baby bonus, then generous monthly payments in year one, smaller payments for the next few years, reduced payments at school age, and a phase-down for older teens.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Design implies spending concentrated on infants and toddlers.

insights.claim: Yglesias acknowledges the universal child benefit at reasonable levels would be incredibly expensive but notes it can scale smoothly, e.g. starting with kids under three.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Phased-in versions are the plausible fiscal path.
insights.locator: To do this at reasonable payment levels

insights.claim: Yglesias proposes a government-funded free or nearly free tier of health care financed by a value-added tax, with most people supplementing via out-of-pocket or private insurance.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A VAT-funded public tier would reshape insurer markets toward supplemental coverage.
insights.locator: The other big thing in this bucket

insights.claim: A VAT to fund health care would be progressive relative to the existing structure of health insurance premiums while being relatively efficient.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Consumption taxation reframed as progressive relative to premiums; possible US VAT debate.

insights.claim: Yglesias says Medicare for All has become an endless factional discourse object that only makes people angry at each other.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Single-payer as branded is politically stalled.

insights.claim: Exposure to violence, including murder, robbery and reckless driving, is a major reason life for poor Americans is tougher than in other developed countries, with large resources spent avoiding it.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Crime reduction has large economic dividends beyond direct losses.

insights.claim: The most dangerous city in France has a lower murder rate than low-crime rural US states like Montana or Nebraska.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Highlights the scale of US violence gap vs. peers.
insights.quote: the most dangerous city in France has a lower murder rate than low-crime rural states like Montana or Nebraska
